paragraphs: AIR addresses what an autonomous agent should do after something goes wrong. Existing safety mechanisms largely try to prevent failures beforehand, leaving fewer capabilities for containing an incident or recovering from it. The paper makes incident response part of the agent’s execution process, so safety work can continue after an initial safeguard has failed.

The framework introduces a specialized language for describing and managing that response. It detects incidents through checks that interpret the current environment and recent context. It then guides the agent to use its tools for containment and recovery. During eradication, it also generates guardrail rules intended to prevent similar incidents in later executions.

Across three representative agent types, reported success rates exceed 90% for detection, remediation, and eradication. Additional experiments support the contribution of the main design components and report timely responses with moderate overhead. Generated rules can approach developer-written rules in effectiveness across domains. These findings support incident response as a practical addition to agent safety, with recovery and future prevention connected in one workflow.
icml-2026-air-improving-agent-safety-thr.tldr: AIR integrates incident detection, tool-based recovery, and guardrail generation into agents, reporting over 90% success across three response stages.

paragraphs: AutoVSR turns circuit schematic images into mathematical expressions describing circuit behavior. This requires two kinds of correctness: interpreting the components and connections in a picture, and carrying out a valid sequence of symbolic derivations. An error in the reconstructed circuit can undermine the reasoning that follows, even if the algebra itself is sound.

The framework connects visual interpretation to symbolic reasoning through an executable intermediate representation. A vision-language model constructs this representation with help from retrieved component rules and verification feedback. A separate planning agent then performs derivations using a library of symbolic tools. This gives the reasoning process a structured circuit description and explicit tools for its successive steps.

On the main expression-generation task, the paper reports accuracy improvements of 30.01–59.45% over end-to-end vision-language approaches and 41.96–51.84% over specialized methods. It also reports better inference cost and computational efficiency than closed-source state-of-the-art vision-language models. The results support combining verified visual reconstruction with tool-supported symbolic derivation for this demanding image-to-expression task.
icml-2026-autovsr-automatic-visual-to-sy.tldr: AutoVSR improves circuit-expression generation by combining verified visual reconstruction with a planning agent that uses symbolic tools.

paragraphs: CAGNN addresses the computational cost of learning successive graph tasks with parameter isolation. These approaches assign model resources to different tasks, but accommodating a growing task stream can require expanding capacity. Existing designs often become more expensive as that capacity increases, creating an efficiency problem alongside the need to learn effectively.

The proposed framework uses an architecture inspired by biological neurons and builds task-specific subnetworks from graph contextual information. It decouples these subnetworks during both training and inference. This reduces the overhead of propagating information through the full network while still allowing knowledge transfer between tasks. The design therefore connects the graph context to which parts of the model participate in a task.

The paper reports that extensive experiments show better effectiveness and computational efficiency than state-of-the-art methods. Its central contribution is an approach intended to keep task processing efficient as overall model capacity grows. The reported findings support organizing computation around task-specific subnetworks while retaining opportunities to share knowledge across the sequence of graph-learning tasks.
icml-2026-capacity-agnostic-parameter-is.tldr: CAGNN uses graph-informed task subnetworks to reduce continual-learning computation while preserving knowledge transfer between tasks.

paragraphs: Copula-SVI improves approximate probabilistic inference when different data instances are strongly related. Mean-field variational inference is scalable because it assumes independence, but that simplification can miss important relationships in a coupled posterior. More structured alternatives can capture dependence, although richer relationships often bring substantial computational costs.

The method combines learned marginal distributions with a vine copula, an explicit construction for connecting those distributions. The vine represents complex dependence through a collection of two-variable factors, making learning and sampling more manageable. It then refines joint samples with Stein updates that move them toward the true posterior. This separates modeling individual distributions from learning how their outcomes vary together.

For efficiency, training uses minibatches of vine edges and a sampling strategy that accounts for variance at different levels. A sparse vine constructed from the same sampled edges also provides an initialization that incorporates dependence. Experiments on constrained clustering and time-series modeling report consistent improvements over strong structured inference baselines, supporting the approach as an efficient way to capture higher-order relationships between instances.
icml-2026-copula-svi-vine-copula-variati.tldr: Copula-SVI combines vine-based dependence modeling with Stein refinement to improve inference on correlated data efficiently.

paragraphs: SceneDiver addresses visual hallucinations in embodied tasks such as navigation and robotic manipulation. The paper identifies a shared difficulty for vision-language and vision-language-action models: separating objects that matter for a task from distracting objects. Simply asking a model to focus on the right objects in one step proves ineffective because choosing those objects already requires understanding the scene.

The method develops that understanding through a coarse-to-fine focus plan. It first builds a holistic scene graph, establishing an organized account of the scene. It then repeatedly recognizes, interprets, and analyzes the scene while breaking the task into simpler subproblems. This uses the longer-term planning strengths of vision-language models to guide attention progressively.

To support fast reactive control, the authors also introduce a lightweight adapter that distills this deliberate focusing ability into vision-language-action models. Evaluations on standard embodied AI benchmarks report substantial reductions in visual hallucinations for both model types while preserving computational efficiency in tasks requiring quick execution. The results connect improved scene interpretation with both planning and responsive action.
icml-2026-dive-into-the-scene-breaking-t.tldr: SceneDiver progressively builds scene understanding to guide visual focus and reduce hallucinations in embodied planning and control.

paragraphs: This paper improves Transformer-based error correction by incorporating the algebraic structure of cyclic codes. Existing neural decoders often process codes as generic sequences, overlooking relationships supplied by the code itself. The authors investigate how those relationships can guide the decoder’s design and reduce the amount of model capacity needed.

Their approach derives interpretable error-correction patterns and hypotheses about relationships between nodes from the codes’ cyclic properties. These connect the code’s structural characteristics to model parameters. The resulting method is designed as a flexible, plug-and-play addition for decoding cyclic codes, making the mathematical structure an explicit part of the neural architecture.

Experiments report an average reduction in bit error rate of an order of magnitude, alongside an approximately 97% reduction in total parameters. Further comparisons provide empirical support for the proposed conjectures. Together, these findings suggest that incorporating code-specific structure can improve both decoding accuracy and compactness. The contribution also illustrates a practical connection between classical coding theory and Transformer design, with the reported benefits established through experiments.
icml-2026-drop-in-circulant-structural-p.tldr: Embedding cyclic-code structure into Transformer decoders yields a reported tenfold average reduction in bit error rate with about 97% fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Analog in-memory computing performs calculations inside resistive arrays, offering an energy-efficient platform for large models. Training is complicated by asymmetric device updates, which can systematically pull weights toward a device-specific symmetric point. That point typically differs from the value preferred by the training objective, so device behavior can bias learning.

Existing approaches commonly assume the symmetric point is known and calibrate the reference to it before training. This calibration requires costly pulses, and remaining estimation errors can hurt performance. The paper provides a theoretical characterization of the pulse cost of calibration and the estimation error that results, making this preparation step itself an object of analysis.

The authors then propose estimating and tracking the symmetric point during model training, and establish convergence guarantees for their method. An enhanced version incorporates chopping and filtering techniques from digital signal processing. Numerical experiments demonstrate efficiency and effectiveness. The work therefore addresses both the cost of obtaining a suitable reference and the consequences of an imperfect reference during learning.
icml-2026-dynamic-symmetric-point-tracki.tldr: Dynamic symmetric-point tracking addresses analog training bias by estimating the device reference during learning, with convergence analysis and numerical validation.

paragraphs: Multimodal image fusion combines complementary information from different image sources. A successful result needs both detailed local structure and a coherent overall appearance. The paper argues that conventional shared representations on two-dimensional feature grids handle local structure well but provide limited control over appearance factors affecting the whole image.

The proposed method adds a compact, one-dimensional token interface from a frozen pretrained image tokenizer. These tokens carry global appearance information, while the existing spatial pathway continues restoring local structure. Selective Token Editing changes or replaces only a small set of critical tokens. This provides a lightweight way to influence global appearance without changing the fusion backbone or introducing additional losses.

Experiments on four commonly used benchmarks report the best overall performance, with consistent improvements across multiple measures of global coherence and local fidelity. The findings support assigning complementary responsibilities to the two representations: spatial features retain detailed structure, and selected tokens provide broader appearance control. The tokenizer serves as an interface for global information rather than taking over image reconstruction.
icml-2026-from-2d-grids-to-1d-tokens-ref.tldr: Selective editing of compact image tokens improves global appearance in multimodal fusion while a spatial pathway preserves local detail.

paragraphs: Functional Attention targets operator learning, where a model learns mappings between functions rather than only between fixed collections of values. Transformer-based approaches often turn a continuous field into discrete tokens and compare those tokens through attention. This representation can overlook the field’s global functional structure, making the choice of representation central to the task.

The proposed method expresses attention as a correspondence between adaptive bases, which provide learned ways to represent functions. Inspired by geometric functional maps, it replaces softmax-based pairwise affinities with structured linear operators. This allows attention to describe relationships at the level of the represented functions and explicitly capture global dependencies in a compact form.

The paper reports that this representation is resolution-invariant and generalizable. Across operator-learning tasks that include solving partial differential equations, three-dimensional segmentation, and regression, Functional Attention can match state-of-the-art performance while remaining robust to different discretizations. The results support functional correspondences as a useful alternative when the same underlying information may be sampled at different resolutions.
icml-2026-functional-attention-from-pair.tldr: Functional Attention models relationships between function representations to capture global structure and remain robust across discretizations.

paragraphs: This paper asks where a language model’s ability to predict answer correctness comes from. Confidence is often treated as self-knowledge, assuming the model has special access to whether its own answer is right. The authors find that self-evaluation generally performs no better than evaluation by an unrelated model, across both trained and training-free approaches.

They investigate an alternative explanation: familiarity with a target model’s historical predictions. Correctness Models incorporate this information, while Generalized Correctness Models learn to predict confidence across multiple language models. The study examines how answer wording, world knowledge, performance history, examples provided in context, and calibration after prediction contribute to the resulting estimates.

Evaluations use Qwen3-8B-based predictors across five model families, three datasets, and a downstream selective-prediction task. The findings support reliable confidence estimation as a skill that can transfer across models by learning historical correctness patterns. This shifts attention toward evidence about how models have performed, while the reported self-evaluation comparison remains a general empirical finding rather than a claim that introspection can never help.
icml-2026-generalized-correctness-models.tldr: The study finds that learning models’ correctness histories supports transferable confidence prediction, while self-evaluation generally offers no advantage over external evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why a multilingual language model sometimes unexpectedly changes languages while generating text. It seeks an internal explanation by identifying which model components contribute to the failure and how they interact. The authors introduce a scalable circuit-discovery framework that causally locates multilingual neurons and groups their functional patterns into interpretable circuits without additional training or manual annotation.

The identified circuit has two interacting regimes. One detects and maintains the identity of the language being spoken; the other retrieves meaning that is shared across languages. In the authors’ account, unintended switching occurs when the semantic regime suppresses the language-maintenance regime and dominates the multilingual circuit. This links an observable generation error to a shift in internal activity.

To test this account, the researchers fine-tune the identified language sub-circuit. They report a 20.8% reduction in code-switching rate while updating approximately 0.019% of all neurons. The paper presents this as a preliminary mechanistic exploration, with the targeted intervention providing evidence that the discovered components offer a useful route for improving multilingual generation.
icml-2026-how-do-language-models-speak-l.tldr: The study links unintended language switching to competition between semantic and language-maintenance circuits, then reduces switching through a small targeted update.

paragraphs: IDFT prepares a federated model for later requests to remove a client’s contribution. Repeated aggregation can entangle that contribution with other clients’ updates, making deletion difficult. The paper aims to make removal faster and more predictable while keeping the resulting model close to one retrained without the deleted client, including when clients have heterogeneous data.

During ordinary FedAvg training, IDFT records influence by splitting updates into shared directions that vary together and a residual trace separable by client. A shrinkage mechanism suppresses components that are difficult to remove. A deletion request then triggers one subtraction and a short anchored repair. The accompanying analysis relates fidelity to retraining to the residual influence that remains unremoved.

Across representative benchmarks and multiple dataset–architecture combinations, IDFT reports the lowest average gap to retraining. It also matches retraining-level forgetting with substantially less communication and computation than history-heavy baselines. These results support designing removability into training itself, so later deletion can use a prepared influence record instead of relying entirely on corrections after training.
icml-2026-influence-disentangled-federat.tldr: IDFT records and separates client influence during federated training, enabling efficient deletion that closely matches retraining without the client.

paragraphs: This paper examines why multimodal language models can choose images based on their position in an input sequence instead of their relevance. In multi-image retrieval, changing the order of candidate images should not change which image best matches the request. Severe position bias undermines that behavior even when the models otherwise perform strongly.

The authors identify a mismatch between output scores and internal attention. The scores used for predictions can be heavily biased by order, while attention remains aligned with relevant visual evidence. They call this Logit-Attention Divergence and use it to motivate a calibration method that draws on attention signals. The method corrects individual cases during inference, needs no training, and uses a minimal calibration set.

On benchmarks based on MS-COCO, the approach substantially improves consistency under reordered inputs and reports state-of-the-art performance, with accuracy improvements exceeding 40% over baselines. Computational overhead is described as negligible. The findings indicate that useful relevance information may already exist internally even when final prediction scores express a strong positional bias.
icml-2026-logit-attention-divergence-mit.tldr: Attention-guided calibration reduces image-order bias by using internal visual evidence that remains informative when output scores are biased.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for interpretable mathematical expressions that explain observed data. Generative methods learn patterns in expressions, but their token-level training objectives differ from evaluation criteria such as fit to a particular dataset and expression complexity. Direct optimization addresses the test problem more immediately, yet faces difficulties including nondifferentiable expressions, local optima, and rapidly increasing cost with dimensionality.

MOD-SR combines distribution learning during training with direct optimization during inference. It generates expressions through gradient-guided diffusion in an embedding space, supported by contrastive learning and representation alignment. This gives the generation process guidance tied to the inference problem while retaining the patterns learned from training data.

The framework also introduces DFEX, a fixed-depth relaxation of expression trees that makes gradient guidance possible through differentiability. Experiments report superior performance across diverse benchmarks. The contribution is the integration of learned expression generation and optimization in one framework, addressing their mismatch through a representation that can receive gradients. The reported results support this combination without establishing that every optimization difficulty is eliminated.
icml-2026-mod-sr-unifying-multimodal-lea.tldr: MOD-SR combines learned expression generation with gradient-guided inference to better connect symbolic regression training with test-time optimization.

paragraphs: This study examines whether removing targeted knowledge from a language model in one language also prevents its retrieval in others. The researchers extend TOFU to five languages and vary the languages used for fine-tuning, unlearning, and querying. This exposes interactions that an English-only evaluation would not capture.

Transfer of unlearning varies substantially. It is strongest between languages sharing scripts and language families, and the language used for unlearning helps predict which query languages show the strongest transfer. Layer-level analysis finds that early representations shared across languages remain largely intact, while unlearning primarily changes later decoding layers. The authors interpret this pattern as evidence suggesting suppression of knowledge rather than its genuine erasure.

A subsequent intervention uses a single direction to steer the model during inference and reverses much of that suppression across languages. It recovers 50% of the unlearned knowledge in Qwen and 90% in Gemma. These findings make both cross-language testing and reversibility relevant to assessing unlearning: reduced answers after an update may coexist with recoverable internal knowledge.
icml-2026-multilingual-unlearning-in-llm.tldr: Multilingual tests find uneven unlearning transfer and substantial reversibility, suggesting that the studied methods often suppress rather than erase knowledge.

paragraphs: This paper studies jailbreak risk when an adversary can query a group of large models to obtain harmful outputs. The scenario broadens the attacker’s opportunities beyond interaction with one model. The authors call it wide-net-casting and argue that it exposes a practical safety risk that has received insufficient attention.

Their analysis examines this scenario and develops a jailbreak method tailored to it. The central contribution is treating access to multiple models as part of the threat being evaluated. This matters because an assessment organized around one target does not directly characterize what an attacker can achieve when several targets are available.

With the tailored method, jailbreak success reaches 100% in some experiments involving models without additional safeguards. Both qualifications matter: the result concerns some experiments and the stated safeguard setting, rather than every model or deployment. The findings motivate including access to groups of models in future safety evaluations and defense research. They establish wide-net-casting as a distinct empirical risk scenario whose scope extends beyond the behavior of any single target.
icml-2026-new-wide-net-casting-jailbreak.tldr: Querying groups of models creates a distinct jailbreak risk, with a tailored attack reaching 100% success in some experiments without additional safeguards.

paragraphs: PixCLIP addresses the difficulty of matching detailed language to precise parts of an image. Longer descriptions and stronger text encoders can improve the language side of alignment, but the paper argues that visual grounding must improve too. Fine-grained matching requires identifying the regions and pixels described by the text.

The authors build an automated annotation pipeline that pairs long descriptions with pixel-level localization. They use it to create LongGRIT, a dataset containing 1.5 million samples. PixCLIP then uses a three-branch alignment framework and a unified training objective to connect image regions with corresponding descriptions at multiple granularities. Its inputs accommodate both visual region prompts and long-form text.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on pixel- and region-level alignment while preserving strong performance on global image–text retrieval. The framework also handles arbitrarily shaped region prompts and long descriptions. These findings support improving the spatial specificity of visual representations alongside textual detail, allowing the same framework to connect language with whole images and with more precisely localized visual content.
icml-2026-pixclip-towards-fine-grained-v.tldr: PixCLIP aligns long descriptions with image regions and pixels, improving fine-grained matching while retaining strong global retrieval performance.

paragraphs: OpticalDNA treats DNA as a structured visual document. The paper argues that reading every position as a one-dimensional token sequence spends computation on low-information background and fits poorly with genomic meaning that can be sparse and discontinuous. Its alternative aims to preserve detailed information using a smaller effective token budget.

The framework renders DNA into visual layouts and trains an OCR-capable vision-language model with a visual DNA encoder and a document decoder. The encoder produces compact tokens from which the visual information can be reconstructed. Prompt-conditioned tasks cover reading, locating regions, retrieving subsequences, and completing masked spans, giving the representation several ways to retain and use genomic detail.

Across diverse genomic benchmarks, OpticalDNA consistently outperforms recent baselines. For sequences up to 450,000 bases, it reports the best overall performance with nearly 20 times fewer effective tokens. It also surpasses models with up to 985 times more activated parameters while tuning only 256,000 parameters. These are distinct efficiency measures: the reported trainable-parameter count describes what is tuned, rather than the entire model size.
icml-2026-rethinking-genomic-modeling-th.tldr: OpticalDNA models DNA as visual documents, reporting strong genomic performance with nearly 20 times fewer effective tokens on long sequences.

paragraphs: SDiD compresses stereo image pairs while aiming to preserve both visual quality and the relationship between their viewpoints. This relationship matters for recovering depth. Existing distortion-focused compression can look poor at low bitrates, while generative compression can produce attractive images whose views are insufficiently consistent for downstream use.

The method shares pretrained diffusion priors across a distributed stereo compression architecture. A prior-alignment module obtains a prior for the main view from the foundation diffusion model. A transformation structure then supports fast perceptual enhancement of the auxiliary view while maintaining consistency. The design connects the enhancement of the two views through their priors, addressing appearance and stereo agreement together.

Experiments across multiple datasets report better perceptual quality than existing methods and accurate depth recovery even at extremely low bitrates. On InStereo2K, SDiD reconstructs pairs with depth information similar to the state-of-the-art baseline using 0.02 rather than 0.06 bits per pixel. That one-third bitrate comparison concerns similar depth information, showing a concrete efficiency benefit for preserving the stereo relationship.
icml-2026-sdid-shared-diffusion-prior-fo.tldr: SDiD shares diffusion priors between stereo views to improve low-bitrate visual quality while preserving depth information.

paragraphs: SG-Gaze explores how encoding physical and geometric structure can help gaze estimation generalize across domains. The broader proposal, physics-as-representation, builds underlying structure into visual features instead of relying only on appearance. For gaze perception, the relevant structure includes the eye’s three-dimensional geometry and the geometric relationships between viewing directions.

The framework learns through two adversarial branches. An analytical branch places appearance features on a spherical manifold aligned with gaze geometry. A model-guided branch reconstructs a three-dimensional eyeball using weak supervision from two-dimensional edges. Together, they encourage a representation that agrees with both structural and geometric constraints.

View-Consistent Regularization adds synthetic viewpoint perturbations and requires gaze vectors and structural projections to transform consistently under rotation. This removes the need for multi-view calibration or explicit three-dimensional labels in the proposed approach. Across 12 challenging cross-domain transfers, experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy and strong generalization. The results support structural consistency and rotation-aware regularization as useful biases for learning gaze representations that extend beyond the appearance patterns of one domain.
icml-2026-seeing-the-unseen-physics-as-r.tldr: SG-Gaze combines eye geometry and rotation-consistent learning to improve cross-domain gaze estimation without explicit 3D labels or multi-view calibration.

paragraphs: Spike-camera autofocus must work with sparse binary measurements that do not provide dependable instantaneous image gradients. Noise and illumination changes can also produce irregular focus responses, undermining conventional measures that expect a single peak. This paper identifies a frequency-domain cue that remains useful during a focus sweep.

As focus improves, spectral energy shifts toward higher frequencies; when the image becomes defocused again, it moves back. CEN measures this migration through a bounded spectral centroid computed from accumulated blocks of spikes. It therefore assesses focus directly from those measurements without reconstructing an image or explicitly extracting edges.

To manage multiple peaks and irregular responses, CEN selects a frequency bound whose response has a clear, localized extremum inside the sweep. It then estimates the peak robustly using a weighted centroid of near-maximum responses. Experiments on a spike-camera dataset report the best overall accuracy and response discriminability across varied scenes, motion types, and illumination patterns. The findings support tracking spectral-energy movement as an effective autofocus signal under these tested conditions.
icml-2026-spike-camera-autofocus-via-fre.tldr: CEN focuses spike cameras by tracking frequency-domain energy shifts, avoiding image reconstruction and handling irregular focus responses.

paragraphs: Parallel diffusion decoding reveals several tokens at once to speed generation, but aggressive parallelism can reduce quality. Rechecking earlier tokens helps, yet existing verification can repeatedly mask a token and then restore exactly the same value. These cycles consume revision effort and remove useful context for drafting other tokens.

COVER separates how a selected token is checked from how it supplies context elsewhere. Within one forward pass, the token is masked for its own leave-one-out verification, while its cached key and value states remain available to other queries. A diagonal correction prevents the checked position from leaking its own information into that verification. This creates two attention views while retaining stable drafting context.

The method also chooses verification candidates using uncertainty, influence on later predictions, and changes in cached states. It adapts how many candidates are checked at each step. Across benchmarks, COVER reports fewer unnecessary revisions and faster decoding while preserving output quality. The findings show the benefit of maintaining useful context while revisiting selected decisions.
icml-2026-stop-the-flip-flop-context-pre.tldr: COVER speeds diffusion decoding by verifying selected tokens while preserving their context for other predictions, reducing wasteful revision cycles.

paragraphs: This paper studies dataset compression through a common evaluation of pruning and distillation. Pruning selects original images, while distillation generates synthetic ones. Because recent distillation methods increasingly rely on original images, the authors build a unified benchmark to examine where the two approaches converge and what produces their benefits.

The benchmark reveals a trade-off involving soft labels. They supply valuable information, but can make image distillation less essential: distilled images do not always outperform randomly selected original subsets. It also finds that current pruning approaches outperform distillation at small dataset sizes. These are findings about the evaluated approaches, including a qualified result about when synthetic images offer an advantage.

The authors consequently explore compression with hard labels, emphasizing image quality and storage efficiency. Their PCA framework selects easy examples using pruning metrics, combines those examples, and applies constrained image augmentation during training. This creates a complementary approach that does not depend on soft labels. The work directs attention to separating the value carried by images from the value supplied by their labels.
icml-2026-unifying-dataset-pruning-and-d.tldr: A unified compression benchmark reveals the influence of soft labels and motivates PCA, a hard-label approach that selects, combines, and augments images.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding reduces language-model inference cost by letting a lightweight model draft tokens for a larger model to verify. Conventional systems largely choose between accepting a draft and fully recomputing it. This paper observes that many rejected tokens can instead be handled correctly by a smaller submodel derived from the verifier.

VIA-SD introduces a hierarchy of verification effort. High-confidence drafts receive direct acceptance, medium-confidence cases use a routed slim verifier for regeneration, and uncertain cases go to the full model. The slim verifier comes from intra-model routing, creating an intermediate level of computation for tokens that need more work than acceptance but less than full verification.

Across four representative tasks and multiple model families, the framework reduces rejection rates by 0.10–0.22 and improves speed by 10–20% over strong speculative-decoding baselines. Relative to decoding without drafting, it reports 2.5–3 times acceleration. It also integrates with existing speculative-decoding frameworks without changing their training procedures. These results suggest that allocating verification resources across several tiers can improve inference efficiency.
icml-2026-via-sd-verification-via-intra-.tldr: VIA-SD adds a routed slim verifier between acceptance and full-model verification, delivering reported speedups over strong speculative-decoding baselines.

paragraphs: WebWorld provides a learned simulator for training web agents. Collecting large amounts of experience directly from the web is constrained by latency, rate limits, and safety risks. The authors train their simulator series using more than one million open-web interactions, supporting reasoning, multiple data formats, and simulated trajectories longer than 30 steps.

They evaluate both the simulation itself and its usefulness for an agent. WebWorld-Bench assesses simulation through dual metrics covering nine dimensions, where WebWorld performs comparably to Gemini-3-Pro. For downstream training, a Qwen3-14B model trained on synthesized trajectories improves by 9.2% on WebArena and reaches performance comparable to GPT-4o. These comparisons concern different roles: simulating environments and acting within them.

The paper also reports effective inference-time search, outperforming GPT-5 in its role as a world model. Beyond web environments, WebWorld exhibits generalization to code, graphical interfaces, and games. Together, the results support large-scale learned simulation as a source of useful agent-training experience and a tool for exploring possible actions during inference.
icml-2026-webworld-a-large-scale-world-m.tldr: WebWorld learns from over one million web interactions to simulate long trajectories that improve agent training and support inference-time search.
